interview_metadata.name: Julio Simmons
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised in Rochester, New York — the 14618 side, near Brighton — in a middle-class German-Irish family. My dad worked as a process engineer at one of the old Kodak subsidiaries, and my mom was a hospital administrator at Strong Memorial, so I grew up around both blueprints and bedpans, so to speak. I spent weekends at the George Eastman Museum and the Strong Museum of Play; those places wired me for this combination of technical curiosity and visual appetite that I've never shaken. I was a restless kid — could focus for six hours on one chemistry problem or one acrylic painting, and then be useless for a week. I went to Monroe Community for two years, transferred to RIT for a B.S. in imaging science, and then eventually did a graduate degree in computational modeling at the University of Rochester. I met my ex-wife Dana at a gallery opening when I was twenty-nine, we married at thirty-two, divorced at forty-five. No kids, which was a mutual decision that I'm still quietly processing. The last few years I've been 'not in the workforce' on paper — really I've been recovering from burnout at a defense-adjacent simulation job, and rebuilding myself as an interdisciplinary facilitator. I paint, I code, I run improv, I write grant applications. That's the short version.

follow_ups.question: What was the neighborhood like when you were a kid?
follow_ups.response: Quiet, tree-lined, a lot of families with one parent in engineering and one in healthcare or education. I walked to Brighton High. We had a cherry tree in the backyard that my dad refused to prune properly, so every July it would drop fruit all over the driveway and my mom would be furious. That's my Rochester childhood in one image.

follow_ups.question: Was the divorce a turning point or more of a long unraveling?
follow_ups.response: It was an unraveling that had one sharp moment. The unraveling was maybe five years of me working too much and her needing more than I could give. The sharp moment was a Tuesday in October — she said 'I don't think we're building the same life anymore' at the kitchen table, and I just knew she was right. I moved out within a month.

follow_ups.question: How did graduate school shape you?
follow_ups.response: It made me rigorous. Before grad school I was a 'vibes' person — I'd paint something, throw some Python at a dataset, and call it insight. After two years with my advisor Dr. Keller tearing apart my model assumptions, I actually know when my creative intuition is being lazy. It's also where I started meditating, because the imposter syndrome almost broke me.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yes — 2021, right after the divorce. I had two offers on the table. One was a senior modeling role at a contractor in Reston, Virginia, six figures, relocation package, the whole thing. The other was basically nothing — a half-time artist-in-residence slot at the Rochester Museum & Science Center, teaching kids how to visualize data with Processing. Everyone sane told me to take the Virginia job. Dana had just moved to Syracuse, I had a mortgage, I was forty-five. But I knew if I took it I'd be dead inside within eighteen months. So I took the residency, burned through my savings for a year, and that's the decision that made me who I am now — the facilitator, the guy applying for maker-space grants. It was terrifying and I still second-guess it at 3 a.m. sometimes, but I'd do it again.

follow_ups.question: What did the first month after that choice feel like?
follow_ups.response: Euphoric for about ten days, then a slow creeping dread. I remember standing in the RMSC parking lot in November eating a gas-station sandwich and thinking 'you idiot, you just turned down a 401(k).' Then I went inside and a twelve-year-old asked me how to make a sine wave draw a flower in p5.js, and I felt okay again.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone support that choice?
follow_ups.response: My friend Marcus — he runs the improv troupe — told me the Virginia job would kill the part of me he liked. And my mom, surprisingly. She said 'your father would have taken the money and regretted it. Don't be your father on this one.' That landed hard.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: Conscious, painfully so. I made a spreadsheet — literally a weighted decision matrix with columns for financial runway, mental health, professional identity, relationship to Rochester. The spreadsheet said Virginia. I overrode the spreadsheet. That's a data person's way of admitting the gut was right.

follow_ups.question: Do you still have the spreadsheet?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, it's in a folder called 'artifacts' on my Dropbox. I look at it about once a year.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Honestly, yes — a decent career counselor who understood creative-STEM hybrid careers would have saved me maybe a year of flailing. And the state should have some kind of transitional grant for mid-career people pivoting into arts-science work. I ended up improvising my own support system out of friends and Reddit.

follow_ups.question: Did therapy help?
follow_ups.response: Yes. My therapist Dr. Liu at Strong Behavioral Health was enormous during that period. She gave me the frame that a 'nervous system in crisis' is not a career advisor, which I needed to hear.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: No partner, no kids. My mom Eleanor is still alive, she's seventy-eight, lives in a condo in Pittsford about twelve minutes from me. We have dinner every Sunday at her place — she makes this pot roast that is objectively mediocre but sacredly important. My dad Robert passed in 2019 from congestive heart failure; that's still a weight I carry. I have one older sister, Catherine, she's fifty-three, lives in Denver with her husband and two teenage kids, Jasper and Nora. We FaceTime every other weekend and I fly out maybe once a year. My ex-wife Dana and I are cordial — we text on each other's birthdays. I was close to her sister Miriam and I miss her more than I miss Dana, honestly. That's the immediate blood-and-marriage map. I think of my improv troupe and my hiking group as chosen family at this point; Marcus and his husband Derek have me over for dinner probably twice a month.

follow_ups.question: What's your relationship with your mom like?
follow_ups.response: Close but wiry. She worries about me constantly. She thinks I should be remarried, employed full-time, and not up at 2 a.m. coding. I think she's allowed to have opinions; I don't have to act on them.

follow_ups.question: Do you want kids?
follow_ups.response: That door is mostly closed for me at forty-nine. Some days I feel clean about it, other days I watch Jasper and Nora on FaceTime and something hurts. I've made peace with the mentor role — teaching teens at the RMSC is part of how I metabolize that.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your sister's kids?
follow_ups.response: In person, once a year, usually around the holidays. Digitally, we play Dungeons & Dragons online one Sunday a month — I'm DMing a campaign for them and two of their friends. That's become really meaningful.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My uncle Declan — my mom's younger brother — lives in Buffalo, we see each other maybe three times a year. He's a retired union pipefitter, great storyteller, terrible at email. That's about it for immediate family.

follow_ups.question: Any cousins you're close with?
follow_ups.response: Declan's daughter Siobhan, she's my age, she's an ER nurse in Buffalo. We text memes.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yeah, a lot. Marcus Reyes is my closest friend — director of the Rochester Fringe improv troupe, we've done Thursday-night rehearsals together for nine years. His husband Derek is a landscape architect and makes the best old-fashioned in Monroe County. Then there's Priya Shah, who I met in grad school; she's a data scientist at RIT now, we meet Saturday mornings at Joe Bean Coffee on University Ave to co-work. My hiking buddies Tom and Rashida — we do at least one Finger Lakes trail a month. And I've been seeing someone named Ellery for about four months, very casually; they're a ceramicist who teaches at MAG. Too early to call that anything, but it's nice.

follow_ups.question: How do you meet new people at this stage of life?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, through the things I'm doing anyway — improv, the frisbee league, the cycling group on the Erie Canal towpath. I'm not on dating apps; Ellery I met at a gallery opening, which is the universe being very on-brand.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Marcus bond over most?
follow_ups.response: He's the one person who can tell when I'm performing confidence versus actually having it. Nine years of improv together will do that. We also both grew up working-class Catholic-ish, so there's a shared nervous system.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Brighton, specifically the 14618, near Twelve Corners. It's an inner-ring suburb of Rochester — leafy, mostly single-family homes built between 1920 and 1960, good sidewalks, excellent library. Demographically it's pretty mixed for Monroe County — a decent Jewish community, a growing South Asian population, a lot of University of Rochester faculty. I can walk to Buckman's Deli, to the Brighton Farmers Market on Sundays from May to November, and to the Brighton branch library. My house is a 1947 Cape Cod that I've been slowly renovating for twelve years. I know my neighbors on both sides — the Kaplans to the east, the Nguyens to the west. It's quiet, maybe too quiet sometimes. The downside is it's a car-dependent suburb for anything beyond the immediate blocks, and property taxes in Monroe County are brutal.

follow_ups.question: What's your favorite thing about the neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: The Brighton Farmers Market, hands down. I know the heirloom-tomato guy, the sourdough woman, the maple-syrup couple. Sunday mornings there are a form of civic church for me.

follow_ups.question: Any downsides beyond taxes?
follow_ups.response: The winters are punishing, and the suburb has almost no late-night life. If I want to do anything past ten p.m. I have to drive to the South Wedge or East End.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: Very safe. I walk at night with headphones on without thinking about it. There was a rash of car break-ins last summer along Winton Road, but nothing violent. Brighton PD is responsive, for better and worse — they respond fast, they also over-police teenagers sometimes.

follow_ups.question: Do you lock your doors at night?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but I admit I forget about one week in three.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: Ups: community, trails, the Eastman School's free concerts, being close to my mom. Downs: the gray season from November to April is legitimately hard on my mental health, and Rochester is economically stuck in ways that make my career plans precarious. I love it and I resent it, which is maybe just what adulthood is.

follow_ups.question: Have you considered moving?
follow_ups.response: Every February. Portland Maine, Asheville, sometimes Pittsburgh. But the roots here are deep.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Just me and my cat Fermi, a seven-year-old black domestic shorthair named after Enrico Fermi because she does experimental physics on my houseplants. It's a two-bedroom Cape, so I've got one bedroom as a bedroom and the other as a studio with my synths, a drawing tablet, and two monitors. Ellery stays over maybe one night a week but doesn't live here. My mom stayed for three weeks last November after a hip procedure, in the studio on a pull-out, but that was temporary.

follow_ups.question: Is living alone a choice you like?
follow_ups.response: Mostly yes. I need a lot of quiet to do the kind of work I do. But there's a loneliness cost that I'm not going to pretend isn't real.

follow_ups.question: Do you want that to change?
follow_ups.response: If Ellery and I keep going, maybe. I'm not rushing it.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Just me and Fermi — both permanent.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Ellery, about once a week. That's it.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Weekdays I'm up at 6:30, meditate for twenty minutes using the Waking Up app, coffee with Priya at Joe Bean on Tuesday and Saturday mornings. Monday I teach an evening workshop at the RMSC from 6 to 8. Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday mornings are my deep-work blocks — grant writing, coding on the p5.js quantum-physics illustrations, painting if the light is good. Thursday night is improv rehearsal at MuCCC 7 to 10. Friday is admin and errands. Saturdays I hike if the weather allows, otherwise studio. Sunday I do the farmers market, then dinner at my mom's, then the D&D game with my niece and nephew from 7 to 10. I try to be in bed by eleven.

follow_ups.question: How strict is this routine?
follow_ups.response: The scaffolding is strict because without it my anxiety eats me. Inside the scaffolding I'm flexible.

follow_ups.question: What happens when the routine breaks?
follow_ups.response: If I miss meditation for more than three days in a row I can feel the wheels coming off. I've learned to treat that as a warning light, not a moral failing.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: Technically I'm not in the workforce — I don't have a W-2 job right now. What I actually do: I have a 1099 contract with the Rochester Museum & Science Center for about eight hours of workshop teaching a week, fall and spring. I have a small arts-council micro-grant for the quantum graphic-novel project. I occasionally take paid speaking gigs — I did a keynote at SUNY Geneseo in February for eight hundred dollars. And I'm drawing down savings. It's a patchwork year, and I'm trying to get the makerspace nonprofit incorporated by fall so I can raise real money.

follow_ups.question: Does the patchwork stress you out?
follow_ups.response: Constantly. It also forces a kind of creative discipline I never had when I had a salary.

follow_ups.question: What would 'made it' look like?
follow_ups.response: A sustainable $60K a year from some combination of the makerspace, workshop fees, and grants. Not rich. Stable.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I volunteer at the RMSC outreach program two Saturdays a month when I'm not hiking — we do science-visualization tables at branch libraries. I'm the treasurer of the improv troupe, which means about four hours of QuickBooks a month. I mow my mom's lawn in summer and shovel her driveway in winter. I'm also the D&D Dungeon Master for my niece and nephew's campaign, which is more prep work than people realize — probably three hours of writing per session.

follow_ups.question: Is the treasurer role stressful?
follow_ups.response: Only at tax time. The troupe is small — nine people, maybe twelve grand a year in revenue — so it's not complicated, just tedious.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Two things. First, I added the Tuesday morning coffee with Priya about three months ago — before that I was becoming a hermit and she intervened. Second, I cut social media down to twenty minutes a day using the one-sec app. That freed up probably an hour a day that now goes into actual drawing. Both changes have been net positive; my mood is measurably better since January.

follow_ups.question: How do you measure mood?
follow_ups.response: I literally keep a mood log in a Notion database — 1 to 10, morning and evening, since 2022. Occupational hazard of being a data person.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I don't have kids. If it helps — my niece Nora is in marching band and my nephew Jasper is on the high school debate team and plays Minecraft competitively, if that's a thing. But they're in Denver, so I only know this secondhand.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Minimal and uneventful, which I know is a privilege linked to how I read to cops. A few speeding tickets on 490 between 2008 and 2015. One DUI checkpoint where I was waved through. I called Brighton PD once in 2022 when a car alarm was going off at 3 a.m. in front of my house for an hour — they came, handled it. That's really it. I've never been arrested or detained.

follow_ups.question: How do you feel about police generally?
follow_ups.response: Complicated. I think local Brighton PD is mostly fine. I think the broader American institution of policing needs deep structural reform. Those can both be true.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: I was at the 2020 BLM march on East Avenue when Rochester PD used pepper spray on a crowd that included my friend Marcus. He was okay but shaken. That shifted my politics noticeably.

follow_ups.question: Did you go to more protests after?
follow_ups.response: Three more that summer, then I burned out and started donating to bail funds instead.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: One friend from grad school was arrested at an Occupy protest in 2011, held for about eighteen hours, charges dropped. No one in my family. I've never been arrested.

follow_ups.question: Did that friend's experience affect you?
follow_ups.response: It was my first real education in how the system actually treats protest.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in every single election — federal, state, local, school board, even the weird off-cycle county judge races nobody reads about. I register through the Monroe County Board of Elections and I've voted at the Twelve Corners Presbyterian polling place since 2008. I think my voting record is spotless going back twenty years; I'm a little self-righteous about it.

follow_ups.question: Do you do anything beyond voting?
follow_ups.response: I donate to local candidates I believe in — about a thousand dollars a cycle spread across three or four races. I've phone-banked twice, once for a state senate race in 2022 and once for a city council race in 2023. I hate phone-banking.

follow_ups.question: Why do you hate it?
follow_ups.response: I'm better with people in person than on a cold call. I would rather canvass door-to-door, which I also did, for about eight hours in fall 2022.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I'm a pretty committed progressive, to be honest. Economically I'm well to the left of the median Democrat — I support single-payer health care, I think the federal minimum wage should be fifteen minimum and probably indexed to local cost of living, and I'm sympathetic to a wealth tax on the top tenth of a percent. On culture, I'm socially liberal but allergic to the more performative corners of online left discourse; I think the left has sometimes chosen symbolic wins over material ones. On civil liberties I'm pretty absolutist — pro free speech, pro due process, anti surveillance, skeptical of the security state. I'm a strong environmentalist; I've donated to the Sierra Club for fifteen years and I pay extra for renewable energy through RG&E. I care a lot about local politics — I read the Democrat & Chronicle every morning. My trust in national institutions is low and declining; my trust in my actual neighbors is higher than it used to be. I voted Democrat in every presidential since 1996 but I've voted third-party and independent in local races when the Democratic candidate was a machine hack. I'd call myself a progressive Democrat with libertarian tendencies on speech and privacy and an institutionalist streak that's fraying.

follow_ups.question: What issue are you most intense about?
follow_ups.response: Climate, probably. It's the one that keeps me up at night. After that, housing affordability — Rochester is still affordable but the trend is bad.

follow_ups.question: Any issues you've changed your mind on?
follow_ups.response: I used to be a pretty uncritical free-trader. Watching Rochester's manufacturing base hollow out in my lifetime, including the company my dad worked for, made me rethink a lot.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: In the last two years I've become more skeptical of big-tech platforms and more open to antitrust enforcement — watching what social media is doing to teenagers, including my nephew, radicalized me on that. I've also gotten more serious about local politics and less emotionally invested in national politics; I think the national stuff is mostly theater at this point and the actual leverage is in school boards, city councils, state legislatures. I've softened a little on gun policy — I still support universal background checks and red-flag laws, but I don't think a federal AR-15 ban is politically achievable or the top priority anymore.

follow_ups.question: What caused the local-politics shift?
follow_ups.response: Watching the Rochester city school district fall apart and realizing my federal donations were rounding errors but a $500 donation to a school board candidate was consequential.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: A lot. Daniel Prude died here in Rochester in March 2020. When the video came out in September that year it was the most traumatic civic moment of my adult life — the mayor, the police chief, the cover-up, the protests. I was at the East Avenue march where Marcus got pepper-sprayed. I read Ta-Nehisi Coates, Isabel Wilkerson, Ibram Kendi. I examined my own assumptions about Rochester, which is the most segregated small city in America by some measures. It definitely changed how I think about civic trust.

follow_ups.question: Did any of the reading stick with you most?
follow_ups.response: Wilkerson's Caste. It gave me a framework I still use.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core demand — that the state stop killing Black people with impunity — is obviously correct and I will defend it without qualification. I think 'defund the police' as a slogan was a strategic disaster that let opponents caricature the movement; the actual policy underneath it, reinvesting in mental-health response and community programs, is sound. I think white people in Brighton like me have a specific responsibility — to push local institutions, to not leave the work to Black organizers, and to put money where our yard signs are. I try to do that. I don't always succeed.

follow_ups.question: Where do you put money?
follow_ups.response: Roc/ACTS, the local bail fund, and two mutual-aid groups. About fifteen hundred a year.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think we're in a backlash cycle and it's going to get worse before it gets better. I think a lot of white liberals, myself included, did a lot of reading in 2020 and then got tired and quiet. I think structural segregation is the load-bearing wall of American inequality and nobody wants to touch it because the housing politics are radioactive. I also think there are real and honest disagreements among Black Americans about what the right strategy is, and white people shouldn't be flattening that.

follow_ups.question: Have you had hard conversations with family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly with an uncle-in-law of my sister's at Thanksgiving. It did not go well.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I've done all three over time — protests in 2020, sustained conversations with friends and family, and ongoing donations and reading. I'm not a public activist; I'm a participant.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Marcus and Derek, both progressive, both active; Derek is Black and has been doing this work longer than I've been paying attention. Priya has been vocal on anti-Asian hate especially. My mom is a sympathetic liberal who doesn't really do activism. My sister in Denver is pretty quiet on it publicly but donates. The uncle-in-law is a Fox News guy and we avoid the topic now.

follow_ups.question: Have you learned from Derek?
follow_ups.response: A lot. He's patient with me when I don't deserve it, and he's also told me when I was being dumb, which I also didn't deserve.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Physically I'm in decent shape for forty-nine — I hike regularly, I cycle in summer, I play ultimate frisbee. Resting heart rate around sixty, BMI around twenty-four. I have generalized anxiety disorder, diagnosed in 2019, managed with a combination of sertraline (100 mg daily), weekly therapy with Dr. Liu, meditation, and exercise. I have a mild lumbar disc issue from a hiking fall in 2021 that flares up maybe twice a year. Otherwise no major chronic conditions. My cholesterol is borderline-high; I'm managing with diet. My eyes are going — I wear readers now, which is a minor indignity.

follow_ups.question: When did the anxiety start?
follow_ups.response: Probably always there, but it got diagnostic-level around the divorce. The job I had before this one — high-pressure defense modeling — made it much worse.

follow_ups.question: What does the meditation practice look like?
follow_ups.response: Twenty minutes every morning using Waking Up, Sam Harris's app. Been consistent for about three years.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy: I can cook, I have time, I live within walking distance of a farmers market, I like exercise. Hard: Rochester winters, my tendency to hyperfocus and skip meals when I'm deep in a project, and a weakness for bourbon when I'm stressed.

follow_ups.question: How much bourbon?
follow_ups.response: Maybe three or four ounces of Four Roses most evenings, more on a bad week. I'm keeping an eye on it.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: My sertraline dose got adjusted up from 75 to 100 mg about fourteen months ago; that was a rough adjustment period, about six weeks of sleep disruption before it stabilized. I had a lumbar flare-up last March that put me on the couch for about ten days. I had a colonoscopy in October — routine screening, clean. And I had a weird cardiology workup last summer for some chest tightness that turned out to be anxiety-related, not cardiac.

follow_ups.question: Was the cardiology scare bad?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Two weeks of stress tests and echocardiograms convinced I was dying. When the cardiologist said 'this is your nervous system, not your heart,' I cried in the parking lot.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: The anxiety was the reason I left my previous job, so in that sense yes, definitively. The back flare-ups knock out maybe two weeks a year. No kids to care for.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, two big ones. My dad's congestive heart failure from 2017 to his death in 2019 — I drove him to a lot of cardiology appointments. And my mom's hip replacement last November, I took three weeks off my own work to be primary support. She healed well, but it was a preview of the next decade of my life, honestly.

follow_ups.question: Do you have siblings to share caregiving?
follow_ups.response: Catherine is in Denver, which means in practice I'm the on-site caregiver. She sends money, which is fine, but the labor falls on me.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I'm on a marketplace ACA plan now, Excellus Silver tier, about $520 a month after subsidies. It's okay. The Rochester provider network is good — URMC is world-class. I've forgone dental work once, a crown I've been putting off for almost two years because it's $1,800 out of pocket. I put off the cardiology follow-up for two months because I was afraid of the bill, which in retrospect was stupid.

follow_ups.question: Is the ACA plan stable?
follow_ups.response: Year to year it's a gamble. Premiums jumped fourteen percent this year. I'm nervous about what happens if subsidies change.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: I do acupuncture maybe four times a year for my back, with a practitioner named Wei Chen in the South Wedge; it helps, the evidence base is mixed, I don't care. I use melatonin for sleep. I drink a lot of turmeric-ginger tea. I've done one silent meditation retreat — Shambhala tradition, three days in the Catskills, 2023. My mom swears by essential oils which I think is nonsense but I don't argue.

follow_ups.question: Would you do another retreat?
follow_ups.response: Yes, planning a five-day one for this fall.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: Drinking, yes — bourbon mostly, occasionally beer. In rough patches I've been up around six or seven drinks a week, which is more than I want. I don't smoke. I quit nicotine in my twenties, had a brief vaping relapse during the divorce that lasted about four months and then I threw the vape away.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever thought about cutting alcohol entirely?
follow_ups.response: Yes, and I've done dry January two years running. I feel better sober. I just also like bourbon.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.

January through March was rough — Seasonal Affective stuff plus a bad back flare — but since April the mood log is averaging about a seven out of ten. The work is meaningful, the relationships are good, the meds are dialed in, the meditation practice is holding. I'm still anxious about money and about whether the makerspace plan is realistic, but it's productive anxiety, not the paralyzing kind. I also feel older in ways I'm learning to respect — the readers, the back, the recovery time after hikes. I'm grieving the athlete I was at thirty without self-pity, mostly.

follow_ups.question: What's been the biggest positive?

follow_ups.question: Biggest worry?

transcript.response: Late February. I got a rejection letter from the Mellon Foundation on a grant I'd spent three months writing. Same week my mom had a cardiology scare that turned out to be nothing. Same week it snowed eighteen inches. I didn't leave the house for four days, ate frozen pizza, didn't meditate, didn't answer texts. Marcus showed up on day five, made me shower, and dragged me to the diner. That broke the spiral.

follow_ups.question: Have you reapplied for the grant?

transcript.response: Yes, diagnosed generalized anxiety disorder since 2019, with a history of depressive episodes particularly in winter. Managed with sertraline, weekly therapy, and behavioral stuff. I'm open about it because I think the silence makes it worse for everyone.

follow_ups.response: No, I keep it off social. I mean with friends, family, and when I teach — if I mention I'm on meds as part of a workshop conversation I don't hide it.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: My mom has her own anxiety, never treated — generational thing. Catherine is the steady one, always has been. Jasper, my nephew, has some ADHD stuff being managed with a therapist and a stimulant.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I was raised Irish Catholic on my mom's side and German Lutheran on my dad's side — 'raised' meaning Christmas and Easter, basically. I stopped identifying as Catholic in my late twenties. I'd call myself spiritual but not religious now, with a Buddhist lean — I do the meditation practice, I've done one Shambhala retreat, I've read a lot of Stephen Batchelor and Thich Nhat Hanh. I don't think I believe in a personal God. I do think there's something in the experience of sustained meditation that points at something real about the nature of mind, and I don't need to make more metaphysical claims than that. I still go to Christmas Eve Mass with my mom at St. Thomas More, because it matters to her and because I like the music.

follow_ups.question: Do you identify with any label?
follow_ups.response: 'Secular Buddhist' is closest. 'Spiritual but not religious' in demographic terms.

follow_ups.question: Is the meditation part of your mental health toolkit or something deeper?
follow_ups.response: Both, increasingly. It started as anxiety management. It's become more than that.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.

follow_ups.question: Why quit Twitter?
follow_ups.response: The vibe shift after the acquisition plus the realization I'd become meaner and dumber on it.

follow_ups.question: Favorite platform?
follow_ups.response: Instagram for visual community, Bluesky for conversation.

transcript.response: No. I get support from actual humans. I did post once on Bluesky about the grant rejection and got some kind replies, but I wouldn't say I sought support there.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Current designation — not in the workforce. Actual work: independent interdisciplinary facilitator. I design and deliver workshops that combine STEM content with creative practice — for example, a six-week course for teens on using Python and p5.js to visualize physics concepts, or a one-day corporate workshop on using generative art to rethink data dashboards. I write grant proposals. I'm building a nonprofit community makerspace from scratch. I consult occasionally on curriculum design. I write and illustrate a serialized quantum-physics graphic novel. Before this, from 2014 to 2020, I was a senior computational modeler at a defense-adjacent firm in Rochester, doing stochastic simulation for logistics problems.

follow_ups.response: Eight hours of MATLAB, three hours of meetings, two hours of feeling like I'd sold my soul. I'm not being flip — that's literally how it felt.

follow_ups.response: Morning deep work on whatever project is closest to a deadline. Afternoon meetings with collaborators or grantmakers. Evening teaching or rehearsal. The texture is completely different.

transcript.response: Probably forty-six weeks if you count any paid work. Closer to thirty-eight if you're strict about it.

transcript.response: No boss. My main RMSC contact is Jenna Park, director of education — we have a good working relationship, warm but professional. My closest work-adjacent relationship is with Priya, who isn't technically a coworker but functions as one.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about how predictable your work schedule is. How would you describe your job in terms of flexibility with your hours?
transcript.response: Maximum flexibility, which is a blessing and a curse. I can structure my own days entirely, which suits my creative work. I can also slide into days where I work sixteen hours or four, depending on mood and deadlines. The RMSC workshop schedule is the one fixed anchor and I'm grateful for it.

transcript.question_text: Some people say it's hard to take or keep a job because of child care. How about for you?
transcript.response: Not applicable — no children.

transcript.question_text: Do you receive any payments or benefits from SNAP, food stamps, housing voucher payments, supplemental security income, or any other programs like that?
transcript.response: No. I receive ACA premium subsidies, which I think technically counts as a federal benefit. Nothing else.

transcript.question_text: What would it be like for you if you had to spend $400 for an emergency? Would you have the money, and if not, how would you get it?

transcript.question_text: Overall, how do you feel about your financial situation?
transcript.response: Anxious but fundamentally stable. I have more assets than income, which is an inversion from most of my life. I have no debt, I own my home, I have health insurance, I have about five years of runway if I'm careful. On the other hand, my earned income is a fraction of what it was, the makerspace is a risk, and one serious medical event could eat a chunk of the buffer. I feel grateful and precarious in the same breath. A lot of weekday mornings I'm doing mental math about whether I've made the right bet. Most evenings I think I have.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: Started at Eastman Kodak in 1969, moved with a spinoff to a company that made medical imaging plates and sensors after the Kodak restructurings in the 2000s. Imaging and film manufacturing broadly.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: Five years from now: the Rochester Interdisciplinary Makerspace — that's my working name, subject to change — is a real 501(c)(3) with a leased space in the South Wedge or the Neighborhood of the Arts, serving maybe 300 members, with a sliding-scale membership so it's accessible. I'm the executive director drawing a modest salary. The quantum-physics graphic novel is two volumes in, published by a small press, maybe optioned for a PBS educational series — I'm dreaming here. I'm still in Brighton, still in the Cape Cod, still meditating, still doing Thursday improv. Ellery and I are either seriously together or amicably not, and I'm clear on which. My mom is still alive and I see her every Sunday. Physically I'm hiking the Adirondack high peaks. Mentally I'm in a sustainable place — not unanxious, but functional. Financially I'm making forty-five to sixty-five thousand a year from a sustainable mix and not drawing down savings. That's the dream. It's pretty modest by certain metrics and huge by others.

follow_ups.question: What would count as failure?
follow_ups.response: Going back to a corporate simulation job out of financial fear. That's my specific failure mode and I know it.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Integrity between my inner life and my outer life — doing work that matches who I actually am. Community — the improv troupe, the hiking group, the Sunday dinners with my mom. Creative rigor — the discipline of making things that are both intellectually honest and aesthetically alive. And mental peace, which I've had to work very hard for and which I don't ever want to take for granted again.
